title: Women in Hinduism: Goddesses, Gurus and Manu
summary: Women in Hinduism explained for IB World Religions SL: compare goddesses, female gurus, dharma, primary texts and the contested Laws of Manu.
body_markdown:
Women in Hinduism cannot be explained by a single verse, goddess or social rule. Hindu traditions include powerful female deities, influential women teachers and poets, and texts restricting women's independence. These elements coexist because Hinduism developed across many communities, languages and historical periods.


For IB World Religions SL, the strongest approach is comparative. Ask who holds authority, which text or practice is being examined, and whether a claim concerns theology, ethical ideals or social life. A goddess may represent ultimate reality without determining human women's rights, while one restrictive legal text cannot summarize every Hindu community.


### A quick study checklist


Before writing an IB response, make sure you can:


- Define *Devī* , *Śakti* , *guru* , *dharma* , *śruti* and *smṛti* .
- Distinguish divine femininity from women's lived social status.
- Compare Shakta, Vaishnava and Shaiva perspectives.
- Refer to the *Devī Māhātmya* , the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* and the *Manusmṛti* .
- Explain why the Laws of Manu are influential but not universally binding.
- Connect evidence to the three fundamental questions and five IB themes.
- Avoid presenting Hinduism as a uniform system.


The[IB World Religions resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) is useful for placing these ideas beside syllabus-aligned Study Notes, Flashcards and Questionbank practice.


### Key concepts for understanding women in Hinduism


*Devī* is the Sanskrit word for “goddess.” *Śakti* means power or energy, especially divine creative power represented as feminine. In Shaktism, a major Hindu tradition centred on the Goddess, Devī can be understood as supreme reality rather than merely the companion of a male deity.


*Brahman* refers to ultimate reality in many traditions, while *ātman* means the self. *Saṃsāra* is the cycle of rebirth shaped by *karma* , and *mokṣa* is liberation from that cycle. *Dharma* can mean duty, right conduct, law or the order sustaining life, depending on context.


A *guru* is a spiritual teacher who transmits knowledge, practice or insight. The term is not inherently male. Authority may arise through textual learning, initiation, exemplary devotion, spiritual realization or community recognition.


Students should also distinguish *śruti* , “that which is heard,” from *smṛti* , “that which is remembered.” The Vedas and Upanishads belong to śruti and commonly receive the highest theoretical status. Epics, Purāṇas and Dharmaśāstra texts belong broadly to smṛti. RevisionDojo's notes on[the sources of Hindu doctrines](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-441-where-the-doctrines-came-from-layers-of-indian-93176/notes) explain why Hindu authority is layered rather than controlled by one book.


### Goddesses and the meaning of divine femininity


Female divinity is central to many forms of Hindu worship. Sarasvatī is associated with learning, Lakṣmī with prosperity and Pārvatī with marriage and ascetic power. Durgā appears as a warrior who defeats forces the gods cannot overcome, while Kālī can embody time, destruction, protection and liberation.


In many Vaishnava or Shaiva settings, a goddess may be understood through her relationship with Viṣṇu or Śiva. Lakṣmī and Pārvatī remain significant, but worship can emphasize divine pairs and complementary powers. *Ardhanārīśvara* , a form combining Śiva and Pārvatī, expresses the interdependence of masculine and feminine principles.


A Shakta interpretation goes further. In the *Devī Māhātmya* , contained within the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* , the Goddess defeats demonic forces and is praised as a supreme, salvific power. For many Shaktas, male deities act through her Śakti. The feminine is therefore not secondary to ultimate reality. It is ultimate reality.


Yet theology and sociology should not be collapsed. Worshipping an all-powerful goddess does not prove that every Hindu society has treated women equally. Religious symbols may challenge social hierarchy, reinforce conventional roles, or do both in different settings. RevisionDojo's[gender and religious experience notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-453-gender-and-religious-experience-home-modern-in-93184/notes) explore this distinction further.

*An IB student discovers why one quotation cannot carry an entire religious tradition.*


### Women as philosophers, devotees and gurus


The textual record includes women as participants in religious inquiry. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4 and 4.5, Maitreyī questions Yājñavalkya about whether wealth can bring immortality. In 3.6 and 3.8, Gārgī Vācaknavī publicly questions him about the foundation of reality. These passages do not establish universal educational equality, but they preserve women as serious philosophical interlocutors.


The bhakti traditions provide another form of authority. *Bhakti* means loving devotion to a deity. Āṇṭāḷ, associated with Tamil Vaishnavism, composed poetry addressed to Viṣṇu. Mīrābāī became renowned for devotion to Kṛṣṇa, while Akka Mahādevī is remembered in the Vīraśaiva or Lingayat tradition for poetry devoted to Śiva.


Devotional surrender sometimes allowed women to resist expectations surrounding marriage, family and elite ritual authority. However, exceptional saints do not necessarily reveal the ordinary freedom available to all women. An exception may expose a boundary precisely because most people could not cross it.


Modern teachers such as Sarada Devi and Anandamayi Ma further demonstrate that women have been recognized as gurus. Their authority was shaped by devotion, discipleship and perceived spiritual realization, not simply by formal office. This makes guru authority a valuable comparison point with scriptural authority.


### The Laws of Manu and the problem of authority


The *Manusmṛti* , often called the Laws of Manu, is a Sanskrit Dharmaśāstra text concerned with conduct, social order, life stages, punishment and ritual duty. Its traditional attribution to Manu should not be treated like modern authorship. It is smṛti rather than śruti, and one Dharmaśāstra among several.


The text contains tensions that matter for women in Hinduism. Manusmṛti 3.55-3.56 instructs households to honour women and associates that honour with family and ritual flourishing. By contrast, 9.3 places a woman under the guardianship of her father, husband and sons at successive life stages and states that she should not be independent.


A traditional contextual reading may interpret guardianship as protection within an interdependent household. From this perspective, the passage assigns responsibilities to male relatives and reflects its historical social structure.


A critical or feminist reading argues that protection without autonomy remains patriarchal control. Honour can depend on women fulfilling prescribed family roles. Praising women therefore does not cancel rules restricting their agency, property, sexuality or movement.


A careful IB answer should not claim that every Hindu obeys Manu. Hindu ethical authority also comes from śruti, other smṛti texts, epics, local customs, teachers, philosophical schools, devotional traditions and modern law. The relationship between *dharma* , *varṇa* and social organization is developed in these[notes on dharma and Hindu society](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-413-dharma-varna-and-the-shape-of-hindu-society/notes) .


### Connecting the topic to the five IB themes


IB theme Connection to women in Hinduism


Rituals Women may perform household pūjā, vows and festival practices, while access to particular roles or sacred spaces varies by community.


Sacred texts Upanishadic dialogues, goddess literature, devotional poetry and the Manusmṛti present different forms of female presence and authority.


Doctrines and beliefs Devī and Śakti raise questions about ultimate reality, divine power and gendered symbolism.


Religious experience Female saints and gurus claim or embody devotion, insight, liberation and direct relationship with the divine.


Ethics and moral conduct Dharma texts and contemporary interpretations debate duty, family, autonomy, equality and justice.


The[Hindu rituals study notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-42-rituals-in-hinduism/notes) and material on[gender, marriage and ritual roles](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-424-gender-and-ritual-womens-roles-marriage-and-th-93169/notes) can help turn these connections into precise evidence.


### Linking women in Hinduism to the fundamental questions


### What is the human condition?


Hindu traditions often describe human beings as living within saṃsāra under the influence of karma, ignorance and attachment. Gender can form part of socially assigned dharma, yet many philosophical accounts locate the deepest self in ātman rather than bodily identity. This creates tension between spiritually transcendent claims and gendered obligations.


### Where are we going?


The ultimate goal is commonly described as mokṣa, although traditions explain liberation differently. Shakta devotees may understand liberation through the Goddess's grace or knowledge of Devī as supreme reality. Bhakti traditions may emphasize a loving relationship with a personal deity. Female saints and gurus raise the question of whether spiritual destiny exceeds social hierarchy.


### How do we get there?


Paths include knowledge ( *jñāna* ), disciplined action ( *karma* ), devotion ( *bhakti* ) and meditation. Family duties may also be treated as religious practice. Women philosophers, poets, ritual practitioners and gurus show that there has never been only one female route through Hindu religious life.


### How to build a balanced IB argument


Begin with a qualified thesis: Hindu traditions can elevate the feminine as divine while maintaining, debating or challenging gender hierarchy in social life. Then compare evidence instead of listing it.


A strong paragraph might place the *Devī Māhātmya* beside Manusmṛti 9.3. The contrast is not simply “positive” versus “negative.” One text concerns divine power and salvation; the other presents social dharma. Ask whether divine status affects human status and why the answer may differ across Shakta, Vaishnava, Shaiva and reform contexts.


Avoid the misconception that one striking quotation explains a whole religion. RevisionDojo's guide to[IB World Religions misconceptions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-misconceptions) and its notes on[interpretation, language and sampradāyas](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-433-interpretation-and-language-darshanas-samprada-93174/notes) are useful here. A *sampradāya* is a teaching tradition or lineage, and different sampradāyas may prioritize different texts and teachers.


RevisionDojo brings the revision process together. Study Notes establish distinctions, Flashcards secure Sanskrit vocabulary, AI Chat tests alternative interpretations, and the Questionbank turns knowledge into argument. Grading tools identify unsupported generalizations, while Predicted Papers and Mock Exams support timed practice. The Coursework Library and Tutors can then help refine comparison, evidence and structure.


The central lesson is modest but powerful: complexity is not a weakness in an IB answer. It is evidence that you understand the subject. Women appear in Hindu traditions as deities, philosophers, poets, household practitioners, gurus and subjects of social regulation. RevisionDojo helps you keep those voices distinct, compare them carefully and shape them into a defensible response.
